files.lesson.md: --- order: 5 unit: expressions node: AC9M7A02 n2 title: When brackets are needed summary: Brackets keep a part together so it is worked out first. If a sentence says to do something to a whole result, such as "add 3, then double it", the expression needs brackets. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "\"Add 4, then double it\" and \"double it, then add 4\" sound alike. They give different answers, and different expressions." connection: group-booking # data/connections/maths.yml (Make on paper and Also used in; documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8146 url: http://127.0.0.1:8146/index.html readySelector: "#sl-n" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: formula.yml#pic, caption: "\"Add 3 to $n$, then double the result\": the brackets keep $n + 3$ together, so $2(n + 3)$. With $n = 4$: $2(4 + 3) = 14$. Without brackets, $2n + 3 = 11$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@formula.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Brackets keep a part together" say: "Brackets keep a part together, so it is worked out first." clip: - caption: { text: "\"Add 3 to n, then double the result.\"", say: "Add three to n, then double the result." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "First step: add 3 to n. That is n + 3.", say: "The first step is n plus three." } - caption: { text: "Double the whole result: brackets keep n + 3 together.", say: "Double the whole result, so brackets keep n plus three together." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "2(n + 3). With n = 4: 4 + 3 = 7, then double: 14.", say: "With four: four plus three is seven, doubled is fourteen." } - click: Make n bigger - caption: { text: "n = 5: 5 + 3 = 8, doubled is 16.", say: "With five: eight, doubled, is sixteen." } - expect: { selector: ".rulework", contains: "T = 2(5 + 3) = 16" } - wait: 1200 --- So far each sentence has been written from left to right. Some sentences need more care: "add 3 to $n$, then double *the result*" doubles the whole of $n + 3$. **Brackets** group that part so it is worked out first. ## Predict: stickers ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to an expression exposes leaving the brackets out, so the doubling only applies to n." check: type: predict q: "Dan has $n$ stickers. He gets 3 more, then doubles the lot. Which expression is the number he ends with?" options: ["$2n + 3$", "$2(n + 3)$", "$n + 6$", "$5n$"] actual: "2(n + 3). He adds 3 first (n + 3), then doubles all of it. 2n + 3 would double only his own stickers and add 3 afterwards." ``` Try Dan with 4 stickers: 4 and 3 more is 7, doubled is 14. Which expression gives 14? ## Run: check the words ```step stage: run insight: "The board follows the words exactly, so its number for n = 4 shows which expression keeps the order of the steps." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#run", height: 400 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $n = 4$. Dan has 4 stickers, gets 3 more and doubles the lot. How many does the board show?", when: "n = 4" } ``` Work out $2 \times 4 + 3$ and $2(4 + 3)$. Which one matches the board? ## Investigate: where do the brackets go? ```step stage: investigate insight: "Brackets go around the part that is done first, when something is then done to the whole result." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Write an expression for \"add 4 to $n$, then multiply the result by 5\"." answer: "5(n + 4)" feedback: - ["5n + 4", "That multiplies only n. The 5 should multiply the whole n + 4: use brackets."] - ["5 + n + 4", "That adds. \"Multiply the result by 5\" means 5 lots of the whole n + 4."] explain: "5(n + 4): the brackets keep n + 4 together. Check with n = 1: 1 + 4 = 5, then × 5 = 25, and 5(1 + 4) = 25." - check: type: question q: "Which expression means \"subtract 3 from $n$, then divide the result by 2\"?" options: ["$\\frac{n - 3}{2}$", "$n - \\frac{3}{2}$", "$\\frac{n}{2} - 3$"] answer: 0 explain: "The whole of n − 3 is divided by 2. The fraction bar works like brackets. Check with n = 11: 11 − 3 = 8, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#jo" text: "Jo writes \"add 2 to $x$, then multiply by 6\". Click the line where she goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: missing-brackets explain: "Line 3: 6x + 2 multiplies only x, then adds 2. To multiply the whole x + 2 by 6 she needs brackets: 6(x + 2). Check with x = 1: 1 + 2 = 3, × 6 = 18, but 6 × 1 + 2 = 8." ``` ### Add 3, then double Here is how to decide where the brackets go. ```worked \text{add 3 to } n, \text{ then double the result} :: Find the step done first, and what is done to its result. n + 3 :: The first step: add 3 to $n$. \text{double the result} :: "The result" is the whole of $n + 3$, not just $n$. 2(n + 3) :: Brackets keep $n + 3$ together, so it is worked out first and then doubled. n = 4: \; 2(4 + 3) = 2 \times 7 = 14 :: Check: add 3 to 4 to get 7, then double it. 2n + 3 :: Compare: this doubles $n$ only and then adds 3. For $n = 4$ it gives 11, not 14. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Jo's working one line at a time. Which operation is done to the whole of $x + 2$? ### Your turn Say the steps, then decide whether a part needs brackets. ## Modify: new sentences ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: subtract first, a sentence that needs no brackets, two letters, and dividing the whole result." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#sub-first", height: 400 } tasks: - starter: "formula.yml#sub-first" check: type: answer q: "Write an expression for \"subtract 2 from $n$, then multiply the result by 3\"." answer: "3(n - 2)" feedback: - ["3n - 2", "That multiplies only n, then subtracts 2. Subtract first, then multiply the whole result: use brackets."] - ["3 - n - 2", "Multiply the whole result by 3."] explain: "3(n − 2). Check with n = 5: 5 − 2 = 3, then × 3 = 9." - starter: "formula.yml#no-brackets" check: type: answer q: "Write an expression for \"multiply $n$ by 3, then add 2\"." answer: "3n + 2" feedback: - ["3(n + 2)", "That adds 2 first. Here n is multiplied first, then 2 is added: no brackets needed."] explain: "3n + 2. Brackets are only needed when a later step applies to a result that was made by an earlier add or subtract." - starter: "formula.yml#two-letters" check: type: answer q: "Write an expression for \"add $a$ and $b$, then multiply the result by 4\"." answer: "4(a + b)" feedback: - ["4a + b", "That multiplies only a. The 4 multiplies the whole sum: use brackets."] explain: "4(a + b). Check with a = 2 and b = 3: 2 + 3 = 5, then × 4 = 20." - starter: "formula.yml#halve" check: type: answer q: "Write an expression for \"add 5 to $n$, then halve the result\"." answer: "(n + 5)/2" feedback: - ["n + 5/2", "That halves only the 5. The whole n + 5 is halved: put it in brackets, or over the fraction bar."] - ["n/2 + 5", "That halves n and then adds 5. Add the 5 first, then halve the whole."] explain: "(n + 5)/2. Check with n = 3: 3 + 5 = 8, then halved is 4." ``` ### Subtract, then multiply The board does what the words say. Write your expression, then check it with a number. ### No brackets ### Two letters ### Halving ## Practise: brackets or not? ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing when brackets are needed, mixed, with one question where they are not; the review is substituting." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Books cost 8 dollars each. Write an expression for the cost of $n$ books after taking 5 dollars off the total." answer: "8n - 5" feedback: - ["8(n - 5)", "The 5 dollars comes off the total after the books are multiplied. No brackets: 8n − 5."] explain: "8n − 5: the books cost 8n, then 5 dollars is taken off." - check: type: answer q: "A group of $n$ adults and 3 children each pay 6 dollars. Write an expression for the total." answer: "6(n + 3)" feedback: - ["6n + 3", "The 3 children pay 6 dollars each too. Everyone pays 6, so multiply the whole group n + 3."] explain: "6(n + 3): the group has n + 3 people and each pays 6 dollars." smaller: check: { type: "answer", q: "How many people are in the group altogether? Write it with $n$.", answer: "n + 3", explain: "$n$ adults and 3 children: $n + 3$ people, and every one of them pays 6." } - check: type: question q: "When $n = 5$, which is bigger, $2(n + 3)$ or $2n + 3$?" options: ["$2(n + 3)$, which is 16", "$2n + 3$, which is 13", "They are the same"] answer: 0 explain: "2(5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 and 2 × 5 + 3 = 13. Brackets change the answer." - check: type: answer q: "Review: find $4(n - 1)$ when $n = 6$." answer: "20" feedback: - ["23", "That is 4 × 6 − 1. Do the brackets first: 6 − 1, then × 4."] explain: "4 × (6 − 1) = 4 × 5 = 20." ``` ### Books ### A group ### Which is bigger? ### Review ## Make: find the rule ```step stage: make insight: "Finding an expression with brackets from a mystery board reverses the lesson: from numbers back to the order of steps." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#make", height: 400 } hint: ["Try n = 1, 2 and 3. How much does T go up each time?", "At n = 1 the board shows 0. What step makes that zero?"] check: type: answer q: "The mystery board follows a rule in $n$. Move $n$ and watch $T$. Write an expression for $T$, using brackets." answer: "5(n - 1)" feedback: - ["5n - 1", "Check n = 1: the board shows 0, but 5 × 1 − 1 = 4."] - ["5(n + 1)", "Check n = 1: the board shows 0, but 5(1 + 1) = 10."] explain: "T = 5(n − 1): subtract 1 from n, then multiply the result by 5." ``` Say the steps in words: what does the rule do first, and what next? Stretch: write a rule of your own with brackets and ask a partner to find it from the board. ## Make: a group booking on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Booking for a group needs brackets because the fee is paid per person; the paper task asks for the expression and the reason for the brackets." hint: ["Everyone pays the ticket and the fee.", "Brackets keep the ticket and fee together."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Five friends each buy a cinema ticket costing $t$ dollars plus a \\$2 booking fee. On paper, write an expression for what they pay altogether, then find it when a ticket is \\$14." steps: - ["Each person pays $t + 2$ dollars", "the ticket plus their own fee"] - ["$5(t + 2)$", "all five pay it, so the whole $t + 2$ is multiplied: brackets"] - ["$5(14 + 2) = 5 \\times 16 = 80$", "put $t = 14$ in, brackets first"] - ["Check: $5 \\times 14 + 5 \\times 2 = 70 + 10 = 80$", "five tickets and five fees"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why are there brackets?" options: - "Everyone pays the fee as well as the ticket, so the whole $t + 2$ is multiplied by 5" - "Brackets are always put around the last two terms" - "The fee is only paid once, so it goes outside" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Brackets go where something is done to a whole result, not just around the last two terms.", "Each ticket has its own fee. The fee is paid five times."] answer: "80" answerLabel: "Total (dollars)" feedback: - ["72", "That is $5t + 2$: only one fee. Everyone pays the fee, so multiply the whole $t + 2$."] - ["16", "That is one person's cost. Five people pay."] criteria: - "I wrote what one person pays before multiplying." - "My expression has brackets, because the 5 multiplies the ticket and the fee." - "I checked 80 a second way." explain: "5(t + 2); when t = 14 that is 5 × 16 = 80 dollars." ``` Do this one in your book. The prices are made up, but real bookings add a fee for every ticket. Write the expression, put in 14, check it a second way, then type the total and choose the reason for the brackets. **Also used in** - **Group bookings.** Three friends each paying a ticket plus a \$5 fee pay $3(t + 5)$ altogether. - **Splitting a bill.** "Add \$8 delivery to the order, then split it between 4" is $\frac{n + 8}{4}$. - **Next lessons.** Expanding brackets, which writes $3(t + 5)$ as $3t + 15$. ```teacher summary: Students decide where brackets belong when a sentence applies a later step to a whole result, and see that brackets change the value (AC9M7A02, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can say which step is done first, and what is then done to its whole result. - I can put brackets around the part that is done first, and leave them out when they are not needed. - I can show with a number that 2(n + 3) and 2n + 3 are different. struggle: Knowing when brackets are needed. Some students leave them out (6x + 2 for 'add 2, then multiply by 6'), and others put them everywhere. Ask 'is something done to a whole result here?' and test the expression with one number. before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. They hide the formula: the board does what the words say, so students check their brackets against it. The new move is brackets as "do this part first". The common error is leaving them out (Jo's mistake: 6x + 2), so the multiplier only reaches the x. Always check with one number: add 2 to 1 and multiply by 6 is 18, but 6 × 1 + 2 is 8. Not every sentence needs brackets. The 'books' and 'multiply then add' questions are there on purpose: when a later step is add or subtract, no brackets are needed. Ask: "what is done to what?" running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Ask students to try 4 stickers on each option." - "Run: ask them to say which of 2 × 4 + 3 and 2(4 + 3) the board matches, and why." - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Underline the part done first, then bracket it." - "Modify: before the no-brackets task, ask 'is anything done to a whole result here?'" - "Make: ask students to say the steps in words before they check their expression." - "Paper: the group booking is worked in books (one person's cost, the expression, then put in 14). The page marks 80 and the reason for the brackets. Books out, then look at the page for the model." stuck: - see: A student writes 6x + 2 for 'add 2, then multiply by 6' (Jo's mistake). ask: Try x = 1 in the words and in your expression. Do they agree? fix: "To multiply the whole x + 2, put x + 2 in brackets: 6(x + 2)." - see: A student puts brackets everywhere (8(n − 5) for 'take 5 off the total'). ask: "What is the 5 taken off: n, or the cost of all the books?" fix: Brackets are for a part that is done first and then has something done to it. Here 8n is made first, then 5 is taken off. stretch: Write 'double n, then add 3 more than n' in two ways. Which words need brackets? Test both with n = 5. support: "Give a two-step frame: Step 1 (done first): ___; Step 2 (done to the result): ___. Then write the expression." leads: > Next: an expression for a whole situation, where you say what the letter stands for. Brackets come back when expressions are expanded and factorised (Year 8) and in Equations with brackets. exit: q: "Write an expression for: (a) add 6 to n, then multiply by 3; (b) multiply n by 3, then add 6. Which one gives 15 when n = 3?" a: "(a) 3(n + 6); (b) 3n + 6. (b): 3 × 3 + 6 = 15; (a) gives 27." explain: > **Brackets** group a part so it is worked out first. If a sentence says to do something to the whole result of an earlier step, put that earlier step in brackets. "Add 3 to n, then double the result" is $2(n + 3)$. If the later step is adding or subtracting, brackets are not needed: "double n, then add 3" is $2n + 3$. The two are different. With $n = 4$: $2(n + 3) = 14$ and $2n + 3 = 11$. ```
